meta.titre: The Genetic Code: Codons, Anticodons and Mutations
meta.sous_theme: Triplet code, translation and effects of mutations

sections.contenu_markdown: A farmer in Bamenda selects cocoyam plants that resist a leaf disease and sells the suckers to neighbours. The resistance is passed on because a gene carries instructions written in a four-letter code of bases. Every cell reads this code in the same way, three bases at a time, to build proteins from amino acids. The GCE paper asks you to use the code to count bases, to translate sequences and to predict the effect of a mutation.

items: DNA is made of the bases A, T, C and G; RNA contains A, U, C and G.
Complementary base pairing joins A with T (or U) and C with G.
Proteins are polypeptides made of amino acids.
Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA template, and translation uses mRNA to make a polypeptide at a ribosome.

sections.titre: The genetic code and how it is read
sections.contenu_markdown:
The **genetic code** is the set of rules by which the sequence of bases in DNA, copied as mRNA, determines the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.

- The code is a **triplet code**: three bases, called a **codon**, specify one amino acid. Four bases taken one at a time give only $4$ codes and taken two at a time $4^2=16$, which is too few for $20$ amino acids, whereas triplets give $4^3=64$.
- It is **degenerate**: most amino acids are coded by more than one codon, so $61$ codons code for $20$ amino acids. The code is **not ambiguous**: each codon codes for only one amino acid.
- It is **non-overlapping** and has no punctuation between codons: the bases are read in sequence, three at a time, from a fixed starting point.
- It is **universal**: with very few exceptions the same codon codes for the same amino acid in all organisms.
- It includes a **start codon**, AUG (methionine), and three **stop codons**, UAA, UAG and UGA, which code for no amino acid.

**Where each term is found.** The **codon** is a triplet of bases on **mRNA**. The **anticodon** is a triplet of bases on **tRNA**, complementary to the codon. During translation the anticodon pairs with the codon, so the tRNA brings the correct amino acid. The DNA triplet on the **template strand** is complementary to the mRNA codon, so it has the same sequence as the tRNA anticodon, except that U replaces T (the anticodon is written $3'$ to $5'$ here so that it lines up under the codon).

**Counting bases.** A polypeptide of $n$ amino acids is coded by $3n$ bases on the coding region of one DNA strand, plus $3$ more for the stop codon. In mRNA, uracil (U) replaces thymine (T).

| | DNA template | mRNA | tRNA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triplet name | Triplet | Codon | Anticodon |
| Example | TAC | AUG | UAC |

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why some base changes do not alter a protein
variantes.contenu_markdown: Codons for the same amino acid usually differ in the **third base** only. For example GAA and GAG both code for glutamic acid, and CCU, CCC, CCA and CCG all code for proline. A change in the third base is therefore often a **silent mutation**, which gives the same amino acid and no change to the protein.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a base is replaced, added or deleted in a gene
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Substitution**: one base replaced. It can be silent (same amino acid), **missense** (a different amino acid) or **nonsense** (a stop codon appears, so the chain ends early). In sickle cell anaemia the coding triplet GAG for glutamic acid becomes GTG, so the mRNA codon changes from GAG to GUG and valine replaces glutamic acid in haemoglobin.
- **Insertion or deletion** of bases that are not a multiple of three causes a **frameshift**: every codon after the change is read differently, so the amino acid sequence from that point is usually completely different.

sections.enonce_markdown: The template strand of a short gene reads $3'$-TAC CGA GTT TTC ATT-$5'$. Use the genetic code to give the mRNA codons, the anticodons of the tRNAs that bring amino acids, and the polypeptide formed. The codons needed are: AUG Met, GCU Ala, CAA Gln, AAG Lys, UAA stop.

etapes.action: Write the mRNA complementary to the template strand.
etapes.justification: mRNA is made by base pairing with the template: A pairs with U, T with A, C with G, and G with C. The mRNA runs $5'$ to $3'$, antiparallel to the template.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Template TAC CGA GTT TTC ATT gives mRNA $5'$-AUG GCU CAA AAG UAA-$3'$

etapes.action: Split into codons and find the start and stop.
etapes.justification: Translation starts at AUG and ends at a stop codon, which has no tRNA.
etapes.resultat_markdown: AUG is the first codon and UAA is the last, a **stop** codon.

etapes.justification: Each codon codes for one amino acid, using the codons supplied.
etapes.resultat_markdown: AUG Met, GCU Ala, CAA Gln, AAG Lys, UAA stop

etapes.justification: Each anticodon is complementary to its codon, so it has the same sequence as the template triplet with U in place of T. There is no tRNA for the stop codon.
Five triplets of the template strand code for 4 amino acids plus a stop.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $5\times3=15$ bases for $4$ amino acids and a stop codon

sections.conclusion_markdown: The polypeptide is **Met-Ala-Gln-Lys**, formed from mRNA AUG GCU CAA AAG UAA with the anticodons **UAC, CGA, GUU and UUC**.

items.erreur_markdown: The codon is found on the transfer RNA.
items.pourquoi_faux: The codon is the triplet on mRNA. The triplet on tRNA is the anticodon, which pairs with the codon.

items.erreur_markdown: The genetic code is degenerate, so one codon can code for several amino acids.
items.pourquoi_faux: Degenerate means that one amino acid can be coded by several codons. A codon always codes for one amino acid only.
items.correction_markdown: The code is **degenerate but not ambiguous**.

items.erreur_markdown: A protein of 100 amino acids needs 100 nucleotides in the gene.
items.pourquoi_faux: Each amino acid needs a codon of three bases, so 100 amino acids need $3\times100=300$ bases in the coding strand, plus three for the stop codon. Counting both DNA strands doubles the total.
items.correction_markdown: Multiply the number of amino acids by **3** and say which strand or strands are being counted.

items.erreur_markdown: mRNA contains thymine and the code AUG is read as ATG.
items.pourquoi_faux: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine. ATG is the DNA triplet; AUG is the mRNA codon.

items.erreur_markdown: A stop codon is carried by a tRNA that adds a special amino acid.
items.pourquoi_faux: Stop codons have no tRNA and code for no amino acid. They signal the release of the polypeptide.
items.correction_markdown: A stop codon **ends** translation; no amino acid is added.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Translate the mRNA sequence $5'$-GCU AAA UGG-$3'$ using this table: GCU Ala, AAA Lys, UGG Trp.
(b) A polypeptide has $85$ amino acids. How many bases are in the coding region of one DNA strand, (i) not counting the stop codon and (ii) counting it?
(c) How many bases is this in total in both strands of the gene, counting the stop codon?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Ala-Lys-Trp**.

(b) (i) $85\times3=$ **255 bases**. (ii) Including the stop codon, $(85+1)\times3=$ **258 bases**.

(c) Both strands: $2\times258=$ **516 bases**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The template strand of a gene reads $3'$-TAC CTT AAA GGA ACT-$5'$. Use these codons: AUG Met, GAA Glu, UUU Phe, CCU Pro, UGA stop.

(a) Write the mRNA sequence.
(b) Write the amino acid sequence.
(c) Write the anticodons of the four tRNAs involved.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Complementary bases give mRNA **$5'$-AUG GAA UUU CCU UGA-$3'$**.

(b) **Met-Glu-Phe-Pro**, then UGA is a stop codon.

(c) Each anticodon is complementary to its codon: **UAC, CUU, AAA, GGA**. There is no tRNA for UGA.

items.enonce_markdown:
A normal mRNA reads $5'$-AUG GAA UUU CCU AAG UGA-$3'$, which codes for Met-Glu-Phe-Pro-Lys. Use these codons: AUG Met, GAA Glu, GAG Glu, GAU Asp, UUU Phe, UUC Phe, CCU Pro, CUA Leu, AAG Lys, AGU Ser, UAA stop, UGA stop.

Predict the effect on the polypeptide of each change, and name the type of mutation.

(a) The third base of the second codon changes from A to G.
(b) The first base of the second codon changes from G to U.
(c) One of the two A bases of the second codon (GAA) is deleted.
(d) Explain why change (c) usually has a more severe effect than change (a).
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The codon becomes GAG, which still codes for glutamic acid: Met-Glu-Phe-Pro-Lys, **no change**. This is a **silent substitution**, made possible by the degenerate code.

(b) The codon becomes UAA, a stop codon, so translation ends after the first amino acid: **Met only**. This is a **nonsense substitution**.

(c) Deleting that A gives AUG GAU UUC CUA AGU GA... so the amino acids are **Met-Asp-Phe-Leu-Ser**, then only GA is left, which is an incomplete codon. Every amino acid after the first is changed, and the original stop codon UGA is no longer read in frame. This is a **deletion causing a frameshift**.

(d) A frameshift changes the reading frame, so every codon after the deletion is altered and the protein is usually non-functional. A silent substitution changes one codon only and, because of degeneracy, may change nothing.

items_markdown: The code is a **triplet** code: $4^3=64$ codons, of which $61$ code for amino acids and $3$ are stop codons.
It is **degenerate** (several codons per amino acid), **non-overlapping** and almost **universal**.
The **codon** is on mRNA; the **anticodon** is on tRNA and is complementary to the codon.
A polypeptide of $n$ amino acids needs $3n$ bases in the coding region of a strand, plus $3$ for the stop codon.
A frameshift from an insertion or deletion is usually more harmful than a substitution, which may be silent.
